Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

A preliminary assessment of the post-wildfire hazards of the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton this past summer show that homes, highways, and infrastructure such as the CN rail line and a BC Hydro substation are at elevated risk from flooding, debris flows, and landslides in the fire’s aftermath. The Pear Lake wildfire was reported on July 17, and was not declared under control until Sept. 14. It burned a total area of 165,909 hectares (1,659 square kilometres), forced the evacuation of thousands of residents, and destroyed more than 120 structures, including homes. The report — dated Oct. 8 and released on Nov. 9 — is largely based on aerial reconnaissance carried out in August. The report’s author, geomorphologist Sarah Crookshanks, notes that it was prepared on an expedited basis so that a Level 4 Detailed Assessment can be started. The fire affected 28 watersheds, with some seeing up to 99 per cent of their area burned. The Clinton Creek watershed (6,663 hectares) saw 86 per cent of its area burned, with 76 per cent of that burned at moderate or high severity. Some 50 per cent of the Big Bar Creek watershed (45,156 hectares in total) was burned, and 41 per cent of the Maiden Creek watershed (5,955 hectares) was burned. The report states that potential elements at risk include residential structures on private properties; First Nations lands; the Highway 97 and Highway 99 corridors; secondary public roads, including the Clinton-Pavilion Road and the southern part of Jesmond Road; provincial parks at Marble Range, Big Bar Lake, Downing, and Chasm; the CN rail mainline; the BC Hydro transmission line and substation near Kelly Lake; and water resources and infrastructure in the Clinton Community Watershed.

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

Type 2 diabetes can progress for years without clear symptoms; when blood glucose remains high, it can cause cardiovascular, kidney, vision, and nerve damage. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: [frontpageafricaonline.com] COP31 draft proposes $120 billion in annual adaptation finance by 2035
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A draft COP31 agreement proposes at least $120 billion a year in adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, alongside accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20. African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Quebec court suspends province’s exemption from Crown oath
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers suspended the province’s 2022 exemption from the Crown oath required of lawmakers across Canada, saying Quebec could not change the constitutional requirement on its own. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will appeal. The dispute could affect the legal standing of legislation passed by Quebec’s newly elected assembly, while the underlying challenge has yet to be heard on its merits. Ottawa lawyer Lawrence David, who brought the case, says the oath requirement applies to the King as Canada’s head of state. Laval University constitutional law professor Patrick Taillon argues that courts could temporarily preserve laws later found invalid, citing a Supreme Court remedy in a Manitoba language case. Quebec’s legislature is scheduled to resume Dec. 1.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

items.title: [traficom.fi] Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration, water and energy control systems
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyber incidents targeting operational technology (OT) systems—the controllers that monitor and operate physical equipment—have disrupted refrigeration, water and energy operations, often through exposed or outdated devices. Attacks on European supermarket refrigeration systems caused food spoilage, while incidents affecting U.S. water utilities and Polish energy organizations disrupted monitoring and control. French industry estimates put food waste and structural damage from the refrigeration attacks at tens of millions of euros. Isolating a compromised system can cut operators off from equipment-status information they need to make safe decisions, according to a Communications of the ACM contributor. Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency said household smart devices were not targets in the European refrigeration attacks, but advised users to secure routers and connected devices.

items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

items.title: [Fast Company] A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. 

This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running.

Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? 

Too rare

Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. 

That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. 

Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. 

Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. 

Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available.

If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? 

The AI factor

AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up.

Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. 

Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. 

Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited.

The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes.

The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out.

Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland.

Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers of its Belgian stores hit. Acting on the first warning helped Carrefour blunt the next attack.

Some retailers left their refrigeration systems exposed. That’s unacceptable. But even with tighter security, you still need a way to trade when the systems you depend on go dark.

What to do

Protect the operations you can least afford to lose. Then drill your teams on how to keep them running through an attack. When the malware designated NotPetya hit Maersk in 2017, the shipping giant handled about 80% of its usual volume manually. Staff taped paperwork to containers and took orders through personal Gmail accounts.

Consider a distribution center that needs to keep essential goods moving. Ask one team to fulfill a handful of priority orders without its usual order system or company email. Can staff confirm orders using a secure offline list and an agreed backup channel, check stock by hand and arrange transport? Have them log each dispatch on paper and check those logs against the order system once it’s back online.

When the drill ends, ask how much of the usual workload the team handled safely, for how long, and where it got stuck. Give each fix an owner and a deadline, then run the drill again.

Find out how long you can keep serving customers with your systems down. A real attack is a brutal way to get the answer.

items.title: [bloomberg.com] ECB chief warns inflation will remain high as December rate decision nears
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said inflation is likely to remain high in coming quarters, warning that a prolonged period of high prices would increase risks to the bank’s medium-term target. Euro-area headline inflation reached 4% in October, according to To Vima, while core inflation held at 2.5%, according to Globo. Lagarde said the ECB will examine detailed data before its December interest-rate decision; she did not commit to another increase. Several ECB officials have signaled that a further quarter-point increase is possible, following two such moves since energy costs surged after the war in Iran. But Lagarde said wage agreements and companies’ pay expectations have not indicated inflationary pressures beyond those the bank had projected. She also said energy-price futures and long-term interest rates have risen since the ECB’s September forecasts, potentially affecting both inflation and growth.

European Central Bank policymakers held the deposit rate at 2.5% on Oct. 29, but President Christine Lagarde said they had seriously discussed a rate increase as energy prices and bond yields tightened financing conditions for households and businesses. Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, and average 10-year government bond yields had risen about 35 basis points since the ECB’s September forecast. France’s 10-year borrowing cost topped 5% last week for the first time since 2002. The same day, Lagarde said she would leave the Frankfurt-based central bank on Feb. 7, 2027, before the end of her eight-year term, saying she wanted to speak on issues beyond monetary policy. Her departure opens a contest to lead the institution that sets interest rates across the euro area. Markets showed little reaction to the announcement, with analysts saying the ECB’s established practices were likely to outlast its president. Investors were pricing in three further rate increases by the end of 2027, which would bring the deposit rate to 3.25%. The ECB’s next policy meeting is scheduled for Dec. 17.

items.title: [elpais.com] Leo XIV denounces racism against Afro-Peruvians and recalls slavery
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV denounced the discrimination that Afro-Peruvians continue to face on November 14 and recalled the slavery and humiliation suffered by their ancestors. He did so during a meeting in Zaña, a town in northern Peru recognized as a site commemorating slavery and African cultural heritage. Leo expressed his affection for the community and spoke about crime, extortion, and insecurity affecting families in the area. The pontiff, who was bishop of the Diocese of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, closed in Zaña the Jubilee Year marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. In May, in his first encyclical, he had apologized on behalf of the Church for the role previous pontiffs played in legitimizing slavery in the Americas and for failing to condemn it for centuries. At the meeting, Analí Montenegro Mendoza, representative of the Afro-Peruvian community in the diocese, called for a Church in which no one feels inferior because of their skin color, history, or culture. Peru is the final stop on Leo's South American tour, which includes Argentina and Uruguay; he is expected to remain in the country until Monday, November 16.
